title: Predicate
definition: The part of a clause that makes an assertion about the [term:subject] and determines the clause's argument structure. Dixon (§11.1–2) is emphatic: 'predicate' in its grammatical sense covers intransitive predicate, transitive predicate, and the [term:copula] of a copula construction — but it does NOT include the [term:copula-complement]. In 'The river is wide', the predicate is the copula 'is' (which carries tense); 'wide' is the copula complement (CC), an argument of that predicate. Calling 'wide' a 'nominal predicate' (a common error) misidentifies the grammatical relation. In [term:verbless-clause]s, a noun or adjective directly heads an intransitive predicate without a copula — this is structurally different from copula complement function. The class of word that heads a predicate is typically the verb, but in many languages nouns may also head (usually intransitive) predicates: this is the secondary function of nouns in Dixon's Schemes II and IV (see [term:word-class] and [term:omnipredicative]). Predicates of being — [term:equative-predicate], [term:classification-predicate], [term:descriptive-predicate], [term:locative-predicate], [term:existential-predicate], and [term:possessive-predicate] — form a typologically important subtype realized through diverse strategies.

examples.notes: Dixon Scheme IV: verb ʔi:h 'be.large' in its primary function as predicate head (with agreement suffix -ma:); noun qo:ʔas 'man' in its primary function as argument (with article -ʔi:). Both classes can swap slots, but primary functions are most frequent.
